items.stem: In a summary, which of these should usually be left out?
options: The main points relevant to the focus
Examples, quotations, repetition and your own opinions
Points from the second half of the text
items.answer: Examples, quotations, repetition and your own opinions
items.markingKey: A summary records the key points only.

items.stem: Which two of these sentences from the magazine article ‘The Return of the Urban Beekeeper’ contain points relevant to a summary of the benefits of urban beekeeping and the concerns about it? Explain your choice briefly. A: ‘On the flat roof of a bank in central Toronto, eighty thousand bees are hard at work.’ B: “‘People expect city honey to taste of exhaust fumes,’ she laughs.” C: ‘While farmland bees may feed on a single crop for weeks, city bees forage in parks, gardens, balconies and roadside verges, collecting nectar from hundreds of different plants.’ D: ‘She now spends as much time planting wildflowers on rooftops as she does tending her hives.’
items.answer: D and C: they show that keepers can plant wildflowers to provide food and that city bees feed on a wide variety of plants. The others give background or description, not points about the focus.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark for identifying both D and C; 1 mark for explaining their relevance to the benefits of urban beekeeping and the concerns about it.

items.stem: Read the magazine article ‘The Return of the Urban Beekeeper’: “On the flat roof of a bank in central Toronto, eighty thousand bees are hard at work. Their keeper, Grace Lin, climbs a fire escape every Thursday to check the six hives, which produce around 150 jars of honey a year. ‘People expect city honey to taste of exhaust fumes,’ she laughs. ‘In fact, it’s often better than country honey.’ The reason is variety. While farmland bees may feed on a single crop for weeks, city bees forage in parks, gardens, balconies and roadside verges, collecting nectar from hundreds of different plants. Urban beekeeping has boomed over the past decade, but not all experts are delighted. Some ecologists warn that too many honeybee hives in a small area can leave too little food for wild bees, which are often more important pollinators. Lin agrees that numbers must be managed. She now spends as much time planting wildflowers on rooftops as she does tending her hives. ‘A beehive without flowers,’ she says, ‘is just a box of hungry insects.’” Write a summary of the benefits of urban beekeeping and the concerns about it, as described in the text. You must use continuous writing (not note form) and use your own words as far as possible. Your summary should be no more than 100 words.
items.answer: Model summary: Urban beekeeping has benefits: rooftop hives can produce plenty of honey, and because city bees feed on a wide variety of plants, their honey often tastes better than country honey. However, experts are concerned that too many hives can leave too little food for wild bees, which are often more important pollinators. Keepers can reduce this risk by limiting hive numbers and planting wildflowers.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (summary of the benefits of urban beekeeping and the concerns about it, no more than 100 words): Reading 5 marks, Writing 5 marks. Reading – top band (5): a wide range of relevant points, clearly selected and expressed concisely; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: it produces a large amount of honey; city honey can taste better; city bees feed on a wide variety of plants; too many hives can starve wild bees; wild bees matter more for pollination; keepers can plant wildflowers to provide food. Writing: concise, organised, own words, no examples, quotations or comment.

items.stem: Read the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’: “I grew up three streets from the sea and never learned to swim. As a child I told everyone I preferred sandcastles; as a teenager I said swimming was boring; as an adult I simply stopped going to the beach. So when I signed up for beginners’ lessons at the age of forty, I expected to be laughed at. Instead, I found myself in the shallow end with a retired bus driver, two nurses and a nineteen-year-old student who was terrified of putting her face in the water. Our instructor, Hana, was half my age and endlessly patient. ‘Your body wants to float,’ she kept saying. ‘You just have to stop fighting it.’ For four weeks I fought it. I sank like a dropped spanner. Then, one wet Tuesday in March, I lay back, spread my arms and felt the water lift me as gently as a hand under a sleeping child. I stayed there, staring at the steamed-up ceiling, and laughed out loud. Nobody laughed at me. They clapped.” Write a summary of the writer’s experience of the swimming lessons, as described in the text. You must use continuous writing (not note form) and use your own words as far as possible. Your summary should be no more than 120 words.
items.answer: Model summary: When the writer finally signed up for lessons at forty, they feared being mocked. Instead they joined a mixed group of nervous adult beginners taught by a young, very patient instructor. For a month they struggled and kept sinking, but one day in March they managed to float. The experience brought joy rather than embarrassment: the writer laughed with delight, and the other learners applauded.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (summary of the writer’s experience of the swimming lessons, no more than 120 words): Reading 6 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (5–6): a wide range of relevant points, clearly selected and expressed concisely; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5–6): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: expected to be mocked as a forty-year-old beginner; joined a mixed class of other nervous adults; had a young, very patient instructor; struggled and sank for a month; finally floated one day in March; felt joy and was applauded, not mocked. Writing: concise, organised, own words, no examples, quotations or comment.

items.stem: These notes for a summary of how visitors can protect the reef and its wildlife (the leaflet ‘Visiting the Coral Reef Responsibly’) are in a random order: (1) Do not chase or feed animals. (2) Stay three metres from turtles and rays. (3) Use reef-safe sun cream. (4) Do not touch or stand on coral. (5) Take litter, especially plastic, home. (6) Use licensed guides whose boats do not anchor on the reef. Arrange them into a logical order, group them, and write the summary as a short paragraph using suitable connectives.
items.answer: Order: protecting the coral first, then protecting the animals. Model paragraph: To protect the coral, visitors should never touch or stand on it, should use only reef-safe sun cream and should book trips with licensed guides, whose boats moor rather than anchor on the reef. To protect the animals, they should keep at least three metres from turtles and rays, never chase or feed them, and take all litter, especially plastic bags, home.
items.markingKey: Mark points: logical grouping (protecting the coral / protecting the animals); appropriate connectives (e.g. ‘In addition’, ‘However’); all points included in own words; continuous prose.

items.stem: A student has made these notes on the writer’s arguments against too much homework and the changes proposed from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: (1) It barely helps younger pupils. (2) Schools should explain its purpose. (3) Much of it is pointless busywork. (4) Teenagers have far too much. (5) Schools should set less. (6) Beyond an hour it adds stress without benefit. Using the notes, write a summary of the writer’s arguments against too much homework and the changes proposed in continuous prose, organising the points logically. Write no more than 80 words.
items.answer: Model summary: The writer argues that homework barely helps younger pupils and that, beyond about an hour a night, older students gain little while stress increases. Many teenagers do far more than this, and much of it is pointless busywork. Schools should therefore set less homework, make it more purposeful and explain to students why it matters.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (organised summary from notes, 80 words): Reading 5 marks, Writing 5 marks. Reading – top band (5): all points included, logically grouped and linked; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: it barely helps younger pupils; beyond an hour it adds stress without benefit; teenagers have far too much; much of it is pointless busywork; schools should set less; schools should explain its purpose. Writing: grouped by arguments / proposals, linked with connectives, concise.

items.stem: Read the blog ‘Why I Gave Up My Smartphone for a Month’: “Confession: I used to check my phone 140 times a day. I know because an app told me, which is a bit like a biscuit telling you that you eat too many biscuits. So in September I locked my smartphone in a drawer and bought a cheap old phone that could only make calls and send texts. The first week was horrible. I reached for my pocket constantly, like someone feeling for a missing tooth. I got lost twice without a map app, and I missed a friend’s party because the invitation was only on social media. But by week three something had shifted. I was reading actual books on the bus. I slept better — around forty minutes more a night, according to my very old-fashioned diary. Conversations with my flatmates lasted longer than a notification. Am I going back to a smartphone? Honestly, yes; I need it for work. But it now lives in the hallway at night, and the app that counts my checks says I am down to thirty-five. Progress, not perfection.” Write a summary of the benefits and drawbacks of giving up a smartphone, as described in the text. items.stem: These notes for a summary of the difficulties of the journey and the moments that made it bearable (the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’) are in a random order: (1) It was extremely overcrowded. (2) The bus left two hours late. (3) A stranger shared her bread. (4) The journey was very long. (5) Beautiful mountain views. (6) The road ran along terrifying unprotected drops. Arrange them into a logical order, group them, and write the summary as a short paragraph using suitable connectives.
items.answer: Order: difficulties first, then comforts. Model paragraph: The journey was difficult: the bus left two hours late, was severely overcrowded and took eleven hours along a mountain road with frightening, unprotected drops. Two things made it bearable: a kind passenger who shared her bread with the anxious writer, and the beautiful view of snow-covered peaks.
items.markingKey: Mark points: logical grouping (difficulties / comforts); appropriate connectives (e.g. ‘In addition’, ‘However’); all points included in own words; continuous prose.

items.stem: A student has made these notes on what makes the salt flats an unusual place to visit from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’: (1) There is no sign of life or movement. (2) In the dry season the ground forms salt-edged hexagons. (3) Its emptiness is unexpectedly moving. (4) The silence is total. (5) A dazzling white plain stretches to every horizon. (6) In the rainy season it reflects the sky like a vast mirror. Using the notes, write a summary of what makes the salt flats an unusual place to visit in continuous prose, organising the points logically. Write no more than 80 words.
items.answer: Model summary: The salt flats are unusual first because of how they look: a dazzling white plain stretches to every horizon. In the wet season a film of water reflects the sky like an enormous mirror, while in the dry season the ground splits into neat, salt-edged hexagons. Their atmosphere is just as striking. The silence is total, with no wildlife or wind, and this emptiness can be surprisingly moving.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (organised summary from notes, 80 words): Reading 5 marks, Writing 5 marks. Reading – top band (5): all points included, logically grouped and linked; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: a dazzling white plain stretches to every horizon; in the rainy season it reflects the sky like a vast mirror; in the dry season the ground forms salt-edged hexagons; the silence is total; there is no sign of life or movement; its emptiness is unexpectedly moving. Writing: grouped by appearance / atmosphere, linked with connectives, concise.

items.stem: Which two of these sentences from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’ contain points relevant to a summary of the writer’s arguments against too much homework and the changes proposed? items.stem: Read the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’: “Tuesday 14 July. Up at 4.30 again for the beach patrol. Ines and I walked the full three kilometres with red torches — white light confuses the turtles — and found two new nests above the tide line. We marked each one with a numbered stake and logged the GPS position, as we have been taught. Nest 41 had been dug up by a dog during the night. Some eggs were cracked, and the rest lay scattered in the sand like abandoned golf balls. We rescued thirty-two and reburied them in the hatchery enclosure, which took nearly two hours. My back is aching as I write this. In the afternoon I gave the talk for visiting schoolchildren. Last week I mumbled; today they actually asked questions, and one girl wanted to know whether she could volunteer when she is older. I told her yes. I hope I was telling the truth: the project’s funding ends in December, and nobody knows what happens after that.” Write a summary of the tasks the volunteers carry out, as described in the text. You must use continuous writing (not note form) and use your own words as far as possible. Your summary should be no more than 120 words.
items.answer: Model summary: Much of the volunteers’ work happens on the beach. They patrol before dawn, using red torches so that the turtles are not confused, mark each new nest with a numbered stake and record its GPS position. When a nest is disturbed, they rescue the surviving eggs and rebury them inside the protected enclosure. They also educate visitors by giving talks to school groups.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (summary of the tasks the volunteers carry out, no more than 120 words): Reading 6 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (5–6): a wide range of relevant points, clearly selected and expressed concisely; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5–6): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: patrol the beach before dawn; use red torches so as not to confuse turtles; mark new nests with numbered stakes; record each nest’s GPS position; rescue damaged nests and rebury eggs in the enclosure; give talks to visiting schoolchildren. Writing: concise, organised, own words, no examples, quotations or comment.

items.answer: Order: how the writer felt first, then what happened. Model paragraph: When the writer finally signed up for lessons at forty, they feared being mocked. Keepers can reduce this risk by limiting hive numbers and planting wildflowers.
